title: All Teachers Should Be Learners
author: Lee Wheeler
summary: A teacher describes using Anki flashcards to teach himself world geography, applying the same spaced-retrieval methods he preaches to students, and the lessons that emerged: don't interleave initial learning, build a foundation before adding layers, and personal (even 'stupid') mnemonic devices work better than generic ones. He argues that experiencing repeated failure and slow mastery firsthand — rather than only knowing the theory of learning — is what actually changes how teachers teach.
points: His first attempt (capitals, atomic numbers, monarchs, and pi all at once) failed because initial learning should not be interleaved — only practice should be, once foundations exist.
Building a mental map of country locations first, then layering capitals on top, worked because new facts need something to attach to.
Idiosyncratic personal mnemonics ('Bamako' via a private wordplay chain) worked far better than any technique from his professional training.
Being 'genuinely and repeatedly wrong' as an adult learner gave him visceral insight into the 'curse of knowledge' that makes teachers misjudge which steps are hard for students.
He now tells pupils that getting an answer right in the moment is 'necessary. It is nowhere near sufficient' — the real question is whether they'll still have it tomorrow.
quotes: Every teacher I know has sat through training on how children learn. Almost none of us have any recent experience of learning anything ourselves.
Initial learning should not be interleaved. Practice can be interleaved, and should be, once the learning is actually established
Knowledge comes out the way it goes in. I had learned the elements in groups of four, so the only thing I could reliably produce was groups of four.
Pupils have far more respect for a teacher who is visibly learning something, because they can see you have volunteered for the thing they are compelled to do.
It is no longer how do I get this right. It is how do I make sure I still have this tomorrow.
